item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', sections 'Keeping the Metal Bright', 'Keeping the Metal Dark' and 'The Elegant Compromise'
item.question: You are handed a brushed-steel flask and told it should read as a light mid-grey, sitting on a background that reads near-white, in one frame. Using only what this book gives you, how do you get both?
item.answer: Treat the two surfaces as reading different parts of the same source. The flask, being close to a pure direct reflector, responds only to whatever lies inside its family of angles; the background responds to the whole source through diffuse reflection. So one large soft source can serve both: the portion of it covering the family sets the flask's tone, and the whole of it sets the background's. Having more of the source inside the family makes the metal brighter; a source large enough that little of it falls inside makes the background brighter instead. Then use distance as the second control, since the background follows the inverse square law and the metal's direct reflection does not — moving the light closer lifts the background toward white while the flask holds its tone exactly. The book's phrase for this is the elegant compromise, and the claim worth taking from it is that the metal's tone is placeable at any step between black and white independently of the rest of the scene. The bound to watch is the lens: from a close viewpoint the family is wide and the source may only just fill it, in which case the light cannot be moved without the flask's edges going black.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'The Elegant Compromise' for the single-soft-box arrangement, 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light' for both the distance control and the lens bound. The matched spatula frames show the tonal independence directly.
confounders: using two lights and balancing their power, which works but misses that one large source already gives the control
expecting the metal to brighten when the light comes closer
ignoring the lens constraint, which is what makes the control fail from a close viewpoint

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Keeping the Metal Bright'; and 'Flat Metal'
item.question: A large fill light is added well outside the family of angles to lift a polished steel subject that is reading too dark. Nothing happens. Why, and what does that fact buy you elsewhere in the scene?
item.answer: Because polished metal produces almost no diffuse reflection, light coming from any angle other than inside the family of angles has practically no effect on it, regardless of how bright the light is or how long the exposure. The family is a hard boundary rather than a matter of degree. What that buys is the cleanest separation of controls in the book: everything outside the family acts only on the rest of the scene, so the metal's tone can be set entirely by what occupies the family while the background is set independently. It also produces a practical trap the authors flag: the large white target used to FIND the family must be removed before shooting dark metal, because left in place it reflects the general illumination and quietly becomes an additional source inside the family.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'Keeping the Metal Bright' for the statement about off-family light, 'Keeping the Metal Dark' for the test-surface warning. The spatula photographed from outside the family records as solid black on white paper.
confounders: adding more power, which the source says makes no difference
lengthening the exposure, which the source names explicitly as also making no difference
assuming a dulling-sprayed or brushed surface behaves the same way; adding diffuse reflection is exactly what breaks this

item.rationale: SPEC-01 lets an entity declare `allowed_variation: {lighting: true, viewing_angle: true}` alongside the invariants that constitute its identity. This source supplies a physical basis for setting those two flags per surface rather than per product. A matte surface's recorded brightness is independent of viewing angle, so its appearance is close to an identity property. A polished one's is not: what a mirror-like product shows is an image of its surroundings, so the same physical object legitimately looks different from a different angle or in a different room, and its centre will show whatever is in front of it. Declaring viewing_angle variation permissible for a brushed-metal tin and impermissible for a matte carton is a different decision, and the source says why.

applicability.when: declaring which appearance changes count as identity violations for a product entity with reflective surfaces
applicability.limits: The source is describing what a physical camera records from a physical object. Whether a generator's variation across angles corresponds to this physics is unknown and is not claimed. The flags this informs are declarations of intent, not measurements. Treat as extractor inference: the source never discusses identity, invariants, or any specification format.

source_terms: the more common obstacle to achieving that correspondence is not undisciplined execution, but undisciplined imagination
most artists don't daydream about making great art - they daydream about having made great art
item.claim: A finished piece is a test of correspondence between what was imagined and what was executed, and the source states that the commoner cause of failure is the imagination rather than the hand: it is too easy to approach the work believing your materials more malleable, your ideas more compelling and your execution more refined than they are. The frustration of the artist's life, on this account, is not that progress is slow but that the maker imagines it to be fast.

mechanism.text: The euphoria of a perfect sketch or first draft is a fantasy of the finished work rather than an assessment of the material problem, so the wall is hit when the hint has to be converted.

scope.conditions: the passage from a promising start to a finished work

caveats.text: the supporting quotation about the poem in the head always being perfect is Stanley Kunitz's, and the claim about daydreaming is asserted about most artists without a count

source_stated_problems: believing your materials to be more malleable than they really are

positive.description: the euphoria of a perfect thumbnail sketch or first draft, followed by a stone wall converting it into the finished work

intra_source_relations.note: which side of the vision/execution gap usually fails

source_terms: I reject the procedures that I have seen, but I don't undervalue homework and thoroughness.
I hate researches where regular human beings are asked stupid questions. Obviously, you will get a stupid reply.

I don't want to hear stupid answers to stupid questions. I would much rather watch their body language. If they are chatting and not looking at the TV commercial after five seconds, we have lost them.
item.claim: Pandey distinguishes his position carefully: he rejects the research *procedures* he has seen, not homework or thoroughness, and states he has attended more research sessions than most creative people. His objection to the group discussion is that asking people to report a feeling about a pack produces a fabricated answer, and that the first fabrication then propagates round the group as agreement. In place of self-report he proposes direct behavioural observation: discard the headphones, watch body language, and treat a respondent who is chatting and not looking at the commercial after five seconds as lost.

mechanism.text: A respondent asked a question they have no genuine answer to will supply one to save face in front of a group, and subsequent respondents can then agree cheaply. The fabricated answer is then reported as a finding. Observed attention is not subject to that failure because it is not a report.

scope.conditions: Indian agency and client qualitative research as the author encountered it over a career from 1982; focus groups, one-way mirrors, dial meters. He explicitly extends the scepticism to neuro-response research ("Take it easy, folks") without having used it.

caveats.text: the five-second attention criterion is offered in passing and is not a validated threshold; the author proposes no way of checking it

his evidence is a list of his own successful campaigns that he says would have failed research. That is survivorship: campaigns that failed research AND would have failed in market are not counted, and neither are campaigns that passed research and succeeded
the dismissal of neuro-response research is asserted from no stated experience of it
the fabrication-and-propagation mechanism he describes is a real and independently recognised failure of group self-report; the mechanism is stronger than the evidence he gives for his conclusion

the source illustrates this position with a list of his own campaigns he says the procedures would have killed (sk_ppm_0011). That list is offered as illustration and the position does not depend on it: the fabrication-cascade mechanism stands or falls on its own, while the list is counterfactual about tests that were never run. No SPEC-03 relation is recorded between them, because none of the available relations expresses 'is illustrated by'

source_stated_problems: asking people to report feelings they do not have produces fabricated answers that propagate through a group
source_stated_remedies: observe attention and body language rather than collecting self-report

source_terms: Materials are like elementary particles: charged, but indifferent
The knowledge you need to make that fit comes from noticing what really happens as you work
item.claim: Materials seduce with potential and also have limits — ink wants to flow but not across any surface, clay wants to hold a shape but not any shape — and without the maker's participation their potential stays potential. They do exactly what the hands make them do, which is what makes them reliable. The knowledge that closes the gap between the contents of the maker's head and the qualities of the material comes from noticing what actually happens while working: how the material responds, and how that response and resistance suggest new ideas.

mechanism.text: Because materials are real they are reliable, and because they resist they return information the maker's fantasy cannot supply.

scope.conditions: physical or symbolic material worked directly by the maker

caveats.text: the claim that materials do precisely what your hands make them do is stated absolutely, and sits oddly with the same passage's account of materials suggesting new ideas
the closing formulation is quoted from Ben Shahn

source_stated_problems: materials seduce us with their potential
source_stated_remedies: notice what really happens as you work

positive.description: Pablo Casals reported as knowing from the first sound of a cello that it was his instrument
